thesis.question: When can reducing a software platform make AI-assisted development easier to trust?
thesis.claim: Reducing the platform surface can make AI-generated systems easier to trust when it exposes behavior for joint human and agent review while preserving mature abstractions whose expertise and safeguards outweigh their complexity.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that broad frameworks and dependency reuse remain the default answer because saving implementation effort outweighs the added review surface even when generation is cheap.
thesis.so_what: Platform and dependency choices should be judged by how well the team can evaluate, operate, and own the result, not only by how quickly a model can generate it.
thesis.how_why: Fewer hidden behaviors lower the effort of tracing changes and failures, but local replacements also create edge-case and maintenance obligations; evaluation and stewardship determine which choice reduces the total burden.

supporting_claims.claim: Hidden behavior in a changing platform increases the review burden that limits responsible adoption of AI-generated code.
A smaller, regular platform can expose behavior through primitives that agents and human reviewers can inspect together.
Cheaper local generation changes the reuse calculation, but mature expertise can still outweigh the complexity of an abstraction.
Frontend and messaging choices should minimize the platform needed for reliable, reviewable behavior in their particular context.
Reduced platforms make evaluation more tractable only when specifications, tests, observability, and human review accompany the generated behavior.
Human platform stewardship must control sprawl, fragmentation, missed edge cases, and displaced complexity across the whole system.

flow.rationale: Begin with the review burden before proposing reduction. Define the bounded RISC analogy and show inspectable primitives before asking readers to choose them. Keep the legitimate value of dependencies adjacent to the reuse criteria; the frontend and messaging examples then test those criteria. The later economics section generalizes those examples rather than introducing the premise for the first time. Evaluation precedes organizational policy so the policy retains its reliability obligations; human ownership precedes the risks it must control. The reflection questions apply the argument before the final synthesis. Moving examples ahead of the conditions would imply universal minimalism; moving evaluation or stewardship after the close would leave the smallest-reliable-platform recommendation unearned.

hook.content: Software engineering is learning the wrong lesson from AI if the only question is "How much code can we generate?" The harder question is: How much of the generated system can we trust?
